papers.title: New Gate, Weight and Wire Complexity Bounds for Sigmoid Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Feedforward neural networks with sigmoid activations are of fundamental importance in neural computation. However, our understanding of the circuit complexity of such networks for implementing Boolean functions remains limited. The analog output of the sigmoid, along with its transcendental nature, leads to unique mathematical challenges for proving lower bounds. Introducing new techniques, we establish new upper and lower bounds on the complexity of sigmoidal networks computing Boolean functions: We prove nearly tight bounds for the wire complexity of computing PARITY with such networks of constant depth and polynomial-bounded weights. We extend the size lower bound of Kane and Williams [STOC'16] against depth-$3$ threshold circuits, to depth-3 sigmoidal networks with polynomial weights, proving a $\Omega(n^{1.5}/(\log n)^{O(1)})$ size lower bound for computing an explicit function in $\mathsf{P}$. We prove that every symmetric function on $n$ bits can be computed by a depth-$3$ sigmoidal network with $O(n)$ wires and polynomial weights. This stands in stark contrast with threshold circuits of $d=O(1)$ depth, where $n^{1+\alpha_d}$-wire lower bounds are known for $\alpha_d > 0$. We also answer a few fundamental problems related to sigmoidal networks, including proving new simulations and separations between threshold circuits and sigmoidal networks. We establish these results using a variety of techniques, including random restrictions for sigmoid gates, analyzing the average sensitivity of networks with sigmoids, simulation arguments, and using tools from approximation theory, complex analysis, and algebraic geometry.

papers.title: Inapproximability of L1->L2 Subspace Distortion
papers.abstract: We show, assuming NP is not contained in randomized quasipolynomial time, almost polynomial factor inapproximability for maximizing the $\ell_2/\ell_1$ ratio over a real subspace -- a problem also known as subspace distortion. This is a central problem in compressed sensing but also has connections to many areas such as real error correcting codes, dictionary learning, hypercontractive operator norms, small-set expansion, quantum information and random matrix theory. Distortion seems to be at the heart of building inapproximability theory for continuous optimization. Extending our results to the case of $\ell_2/\ell_p$ for all $p<2$ would lead to a near characterization of the convex sets over which one can efficiently and approximately maximize an arbitrary quadratic form. A recurring obstruction appears in hardness considerations of distortion -- how does one use a sparsity measure to test proximity to an exponential sized discrete set over the reals? This issue also appears in a host of other problems that involve measures of sparsity, shortness, density or expansion. We believe hardness of distortion is an intermediate step to understanding the complexity of small-set expansion and quantum separability, both of which are important directions of research. The main insight in our hardness reduction is the construction of a randomized affine linear map $T:\mathbb{R}^n\to \mathbb{R}^m$ such that the distortion of $Tx$ measures proximity to the hypercube $\{\pm 1\}^{n}$. Crucial to our construction is subsampling $x$ at *all* dyadic sample sizes, which gives an inverse polylogarithmic gap. This is a highly non-local tester, and thus departs from the local testing paradigm in PCP theory. Our reduction is also quite succinct, and so it suggests a rather simple distribution of subspaces for which approximately finding a planted sparse vector is intractable.

papers.title: A Dichotomy for Exact Quantum Circuit Amplitudes
papers.abstract: We classify the complexity of exactly computing computational-basis amplitudes for circuits over any fixed finite library of unitary qubit gates, with each gate allowed to act on any ordered tuple of distinct wires. Exact evaluation is polynomial-time computable if all gates permute the computational basis up to phases, all preserve product states, or all become Clifford under a common diagonal one-qubit unitary change of basis on every wire. For every other library, the problem is $\#\mathrm P$-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions. Our proof connects circuit amplitudes to the Boolean Holant classification of tensor contractions on arbitrary graphs. For an algebraic library containing a nonmonomial gate and an entangling gate, we show how to simulate the joint use of a symmetric maximally entangled state and its adjoint at polynomial cost, using only amplitude queries over the original library. This lets us evaluate unrestricted contractions of the resulting gate and boundary tensors. Unitarity and the computational-basis boundaries then restrict the tractable cases to the three forms above. Algebraic specialization extends the dichotomy to arbitrary fixed complex gate entries under a symbolic exact-output convention.

papers.title: Derandomized Sunflowers and Radical Lower Bounds
papers.abstract: Robust Sunflower lemmas imply that any large enough monotone DNF of width $w$ contains a sunflower, i.e., a DNF equivalent to the conjunction of a common core with a DNF that is heavily biased towards $1$. While these lemmas are typically proved in the context of the uniform distribution or i.i.d. distributions, they also hold for $O(w^2)$-wise independent distributions by Bazzi's theorem (Bazzi (SICOMP 2009); Tal (CCC 2017)), which states that width-$w$ DNFs cannot distinguish between such distributions and the uniform distribution. We prove a derandomization of robust sunflower lemmas for $O(w)$-wise independent distributions, which recovers the derandomization above with slightly weaker parameters. Notably, our result also holds for distributions whose marginals are "locally independent" and "approximately identically" distributed. It is not known whether such distributions fool general DNFs, which makes the derandomization via DNF-fooling techniques unavailable. Our proof of this derandomization is via the method of moments, which might be of independent interest. We apply this result to obtain improved separations between non-monotone arithmetic circuits and the radical of monotone circuits. Specifically, we construct an explicit family of multilinear polynomials $P_n$ that have small non-monotone arithmetic circuits such that any power of $P_n$ cannot be computed by monotone arithmetic circuits of sub-exponential size. This improves on a recent result of Cavalar, Fabris, Mukhopadhyay, Srinivasan and Yehudayoff (STOC 2026), who proved a non-explicit separation that was quasipolynomial. Our construction uses Nisan-Wigderson designs with an additional linear-algebraic expansion property.

papers.title: Quantum-Classical Separation in Probability Distribution Transport via Nonlocal Games
papers.abstract: In many-body physics and generative artificial intelligence, locality provides a natural notion of phase equivalence: two quantum states or classical probability distributions are regarded as in the same phase when local dynamics can reversibly transform one into the other. This raises a fundamental question: can local quantum dynamics transport classical probability distributions in ways that local classical dynamics cannot? We establish a quantum-classical separation in distribution transport: two classical distributions can be connected exactly and reversibly by a constant-depth local quantum circuit, whereas classical stochastic transport requires a substantially larger spatial range. We demonstrate this separation explicitly on a one-dimensional chain and develop a general construction principle on graphs, based on nonlocal games. Moreover, the source distribution can itself be generated by a simple local classical process, establishing a quantum advantage in distribution generation as well. Our results reveal a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum local reversibility, even when both the initial and final states are entirely classical.

papers.title: Complexity and precision in quantum associative retrieval
papers.abstract: We show that efficient and high-precision quantum associative retrieval is possible with an exponential complexity advantage with respect to the classical brute force approach and with a polynomial capacity advantage with respect to classical neural network implementations for any number of patterns scaling polynomially in the number of qubits. Both classical neural and quantum associative memories store the patterns in a Hamiltonian; in the classical case the dynamics is irreversible relaxation toward attractors, in the quantum case it is unitary transformations generating an effective thermal distribution, followed by a measurement.

papers.title: An alternate proof of the QMA lower bound for set-size estimation
papers.abstract: In the set-size estimation query task, a query algorithm decides whether an $N$-bit input has Hamming weight $\ge B$ or $\le A$ (with $\ge B$ as the yes instances and $\le A$ as the no instances). When $B = 2A$, this is sometimes called approximate counting. The query complexity for this problem with a quantum witness (i.e., $\mathsf{QMA}$ query bounds) was resolved by Aaronson, Kothari, Kretschmer, and Thaler (CCC 2020) and proved using Laurent polynomials. Here we give a morally similar but distinct proof of the lower bound using the polynomial method.

papers.title: Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits
papers.abstract: Symmetric circuits require every symmetry of the input to extend to an automorphism of the circuit. In the classical setting, their connection to descriptive complexity yields strong unconditional lower bounds. We extend this approach to the quantum model of symmetric computation defined by Castro-Silva, Gur, and Strelchuk (ITCS 2026), proving a tradeoff between circuit size and entanglement width (the smallest $b$ such that, on every computational-basis input, the state after each layer factors into states on at most $b$ qubits each). Our main result identifies a graph property decidable in classical polynomial time that no polynomial-size family of symmetric quantum circuits on $n$-vertex graphs with entanglement width $o(n/\log n)$ can compute. The bound holds for circuits with arbitrary one-qubit and two-qubit gates and unrestricted depth, and remains valid under the weaker notion of symmetry with respect to even permutations of vertices. Our proof is based on a new quantum pebble game based on the partial trace. The resulting indistinguishability theorem transfers classical pebble-game lower bounds to quantum circuits with restricted entanglement. By contrast, without entanglement restrictions, we show that every graph property in BQP can be computed by a uniform family of polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits. Restricting to circuits with no entanglement at all, we show that polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits with entanglement width 1 can compute every graph property definable in fixed-point logic with counting. Finally, we give an efficient symmetric implementation of QAOA for MAX 3XOR, providing a starting point for studying entanglement lower bounds in quantum optimization algorithms.

papers.title: Computational Hardness of Online Stochastic Matching
papers.abstract: In the online stochastic matching problem on a bipartite graph, offline vertices are given in advance, and online requests arrive sequentially from known distributions, each matched immediately and irrevocably to a free neighbor or rejected. Computational hardness results of the optimal online strategy have been known only for instances where online vertices have a fixed arrival order [Papadimitriou et al., 2024]. For random-order arrivals or even i.i.d. arrivals, it has been long open since the problem was proposed [Feldman et al., 2009]. In this paper, we give the first computational hardness results for online stochastic matching with random-order arrivals. In particular, we prove that for known i.i.d. arrivals, computing the online optimum is APX-hard, ruling out a Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme unless P = NP, even in unweighted graphs with two offline neighbors per online vertex. For random-order arrivals, even when there is only one offline node (i.e., the prophet secretary setting), computing the optimal online policy is #P-hard, resolving an open problem since [D\"utting et al., 2023].

papers.title: Integral Tensor Isomorphism via Cubic Rings and Lattice Methods
papers.abstract: We prove that isomorphism of integral $2\times3\times3$ tensors under $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ is decidable in bounded-error quantum polynomial time. For a tensor $T=(A,B)$ with nonzero determinant form $\det(xA-yB)$, we use the parametrization of Wood by balanced modules to reduce the isomorphism problem to principality tests for compatible lattices, and use the algorithms of Bley, Hofmann, and Johnston to solve this in BQP. When the determinant form vanishes identically, we get either an integral $2\times2\times2$ core, or a polynomial kernel vector of degree one or two. The linear-kernel case yields another compatible lattice problem, while the quadratic-kernel case reduces to a fixed system of polynomial congruences and unimodular lifting. A quantifier-elimination argument decides these congruences in deterministic polynomial time given the prime factorization of the modulus, which quantum integer factorization supplies. Finally, we show that zero padding preserves integral $2\times2\times2$ tensor isomorphism, yielding a polynomial-time reduction from real-quadratic principality to the identically singular $2\times3\times3$ problem.

papers.title: Complexity Framework For Forbidden Subgraphs V: Beyond Simple Graphs
papers.abstract: We investigate how allowing self-loops and multi-edges (i.e. moving from simple graphs to pseudographs) impacts the complexity of graph problems on finitely defined monotone graph classes. We do this by extending the C123-framework beyond simple graphs. We use several testbed problems to illustrate some of the new and varied behaviours introduced by the transition to pseudographs. We show that Pseudograph Matching Cut and Pseudograph d-Cut are C123-problems. Consequently, for every finite set HH of simple graphs, we obtain a complete complexity classification for these problems on HH-subgraph-free graphs. This sharply contrasts with their simple-graph counterparts, which are not C123-problems and their complexity remains open even for classes defined by a single forbidden subgraph H. We also show that Pseudograph Stable Cut is not a C123-problem. Nevertheless, for graph classes defined by a single forbidden subgraph, the problem mirrors the C123 classification; this correspondence already fails for sets of size 2. This gives the first example of a problem that aligns with C123-problems for a single forbidden subgraph but not for larger sets. Motivated by the interpretation of Stable Cut as a surjective homomorphism to a partially reflexive path, we also study surjective homomorphisms to partially reflexive cycles on k vertices with one irreflexive vertex. These problems share structural similarities with Pseudograph Stable Cut. We prove that for k at least 6, they are NP-complete on triangle-free pseudographs. However, unlike Pseudograph Stable Cut, they are polynomial-time solvable on all graph classes with bounded-degree.

papers.title: Fixed Sets and the Hardness of Computing Correlated Equilibria
papers.abstract: We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. This challenges the conventional view in game theory that correlated equilibria are more tractable objects than Nash equilibria. From a conceptual standpoint, we connect correlated equilibria to a natural generalization of fixed points, which we call fixed sets. A fixed set of a continuous function $f$ is a nonempty finite set $S$ such that $S \subseteq \operatorname{conv} f(S)$. Our main technical contribution is to prove that computing a fixed set is PPAD-hard even at inverse polynomial precision.

papers.title: Nearly Settling the Complexity of Connected $\varepsilon$-Envy-Free Cake Cutting
papers.abstract: Envy-free cake cutting has been one of the central problems in fair division. In cake cutting, agents' preferences over the cake are accessed through Robertson--Webb (RW) queries. For three or more agents, no algorithm that makes finitely many RW queries can always find a contiguous, exactly envy-free allocation. For contiguous $\varepsilon$-envy-free allocations, however, Hollender and Rubinstein~(JACM, 2025) showed that $\poly(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ RW queries suffice for four agents, leaving open whether such a bound is possible for five or more agents. In this paper, we establish a striking change in query complexity: $\poly(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ RW queries suffice for up to five agents, whereas $(1/\varepsilon)^{\Omega(1)}$ queries are necessary for seven or more agents, even when valuations are additive. Thus, we resolve the five-agent case and, more broadly, determine whether polylogarithmic query complexity is possible for every number of agents except six. We also explore the computational complexity of finding contiguous $\varepsilon$-envy-free allocations. When monotone Lipschitz valuations are given by polynomial-time evaluation procedures (e.g., arithmetic circuits and efficiently computable Turing machines), we show that an $\varepsilon$-envy-free division can be computed in polynomial time for five agents. In contrast, even for additive valuations, finding an $\varepsilon$-envy-free division is UEOPL-hard for every fixed number of agents $n\ge7$ and PPAD-complete for every fixed $n\ge13$.

papers.title: Random Clocks on Computation Paths: How Far Can They Reach, and When Does Stepping Back Help?
papers.abstract: A lookup, a prediction, or a return to a saved state can bring us to a stage of a computation without replaying the intervening steps. We model this access by a random clock, fixed in advance, that moves along a deterministic computation by jumping forward or stepping backward. Each observation costs one unit. We ask which language classes can be recognized with polynomially many observations. For clocks with independent jumps, the resulting class depends primarily on the tail of the forward-jump distribution. We give explicit clocks that recognize exactly $\mathrm{EXP}$, $\mathrm{2EXP}$, and each quasipolynomial class $\mathrm{QP}_k$, with the latter forming a strict hierarchy between $\mathrm{P}$ and $\mathrm{EXP}$. A backward-drifting clock with sufficiently rare long forward jumps recognizes exactly the reverse-definite languages, whose membership is determined by a bounded prefix of the input. Between the reverse-definite languages and $\mathrm{P}$, we construct infinitely many pairwise incomparable classes. Finally, we construct families in which every forward-only clock recognizes only languages in $\mathrm{P}$, while allowing occasional one-step backward moves yields $\mathrm{EXP}$ and larger classes.

papers.title: ETH is Dead, Long Live SH
papers.abstract: Among the recent flood of AI-based mathematical breakthroughs (the "mathpocalypse"), perhaps the biggest bombshells in theoretical computer science were two disproofs of the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), via slightly subexponential algorithms for the classic $k$-Satisfiability problems. After the initial shock, the community quickly began to wonder at the implications: how do the hundreds if not thousands of ETH-based lower bounds in the literature need to change? It turns out, not much -- if we are willing to change the exponents ever so slightly. While Impagliazzo and Paturi's 1999 Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) is false, Stearns and Hunt's 1990 Satisfiability Hypothesis (SH) remains plausible. We prove that SH is equivalent to the recently proposed Weak ETH which rules out $O(2^{n^{1-\varepsilon}})$-time 3SAT algorithms for every constant $\varepsilon>0$, where $n$ is the number of variables. We show that SH (or Weak ETH) preserves the typical process for lower bounds: a polynomial-time reduction from a 3SAT formula of size $s$ (the number of variables plus clauses) to an instance of size $N\le s^{b+o(1)}$, for fixed blowup exponent $b>0$, rules out $O(2^{N^{1/b-\varepsilon}})$-time algorithms for every constant $\varepsilon>0$. By comparison, for an $N=O(s^b)$ blowup, ETH would have ruled out $2^{o(N^{1/b})}$-time algorithms. The framework also yields parameterized lower bounds ruling out a running time of $O(2^{k^{1/b-\varepsilon}})L^{O(1)}$ when the reduction produces an instance of length $L$ with parameter $k\le s^{b+o(1)}$. We also prove equivalence of the analogous counting hypotheses, #SH and Weak ETH, and that they rule out $O(2^{s^{1-\varepsilon}})$-time algorithms for #2SAT formulas of size $s$ for every constant $\varepsilon>0$.
